Palsy
PAWL-zee
noun
A worn-down English form of paralysis, through the Old French paralisie, from the Greek paralusis, “a loosing aside, a slackening”; hence the loss of motion or feeling in the body, the limbs unstrung and useless.

Biblical Definition

The palsy is paralysis — the body slackened and unstrung, the limbs loosed from the will that should command them, so that a man must be carried where he cannot walk. The Gospels are full of such men, for they came to Christ in crowds: “those which were possessed with devils, and those which were lunatick, and those that had the palsy; and he healed them” (Mat 4:24). The great palsy text is the man let down through the roof at Capernaum. Four friends bore him, and finding the door blocked, uncovered the roof and let the bed down before the LORD. “When Jesus saw their faith, he said unto the sick of the palsy, Son, thy sins be forgiven thee” (Mar 2:5). Mark the order: the pardon first, the cure after. The scribes reasoned that none can forgive sins but God only — and they reasoned rightly, and drew the wrong conclusion, for the One before them was God manifest in flesh. So Christ gave them the visible proof of the invisible act: “But that ye may know that the Son of man hath power on earth to forgive sins, (then saith he to the sick of the palsy,) Arise, take up thy bed, and go unto thine house” (Mat 9:6). The healing is the receipt for the pardon. A centurion pleaded the same disease for his servant (Mat 8:6), and at Lydda Peter found Aeneas eight years bedfast and said, Jesus Christ maketh thee whole. The palsied man’s deepest need was never his legs.

Webster 1828 Definition

Paralysis; the loss of motion or feeling in the body or a part of it; the limbs unstrung and useless.

expand to see more

PALSY, the loss or diminution of voluntary motion or of sensation, or of both, in the whole body or in a part; paralysis.

A contracted English form of paralysis, through Old French paralisie, from Greek paralusis, “a loosing aside.”

It names the body that will not obey the will — the man who must be borne by others.

The palsied of Syria were brought to Christ in multitudes and He healed them (Mat 4:24).

At Capernaum the cure of a palsy proved Christ’s authority to forgive sins (Mar 2:5–12).

Key Scripture

Mar 2:5 — "When Jesus saw their faith, he said unto the sick of the palsy, Son, thy sins be forgiven thee."

Mat 9:6 — "But that ye may know that the Son of man hath power on earth to forgive sins, (then saith he to the sick of the palsy,) Arise, take up thy bed, and go unto thine house."

Mar 2:11 — "I say unto thee, Arise, and take up thy bed, and go thy way into thine house."

Mat 8:6 — "And saying, Lord, my servant lieth at home sick of the palsy, grievously tormented."

Modern Corruption

An old word for paralysis; the live corruption is the reversal of Christ’s order — a gospel that offers the bed carried away and never the sins forgiven.

expand to see more

The modern misuse of this history is to keep the miracle and lose the pardon. Whole ministries read Mark 2 as a healing story with a religious preface, and preach a Christ who mends bodies, mends marriages, mends fortunes — and whose word about sin is an embarrassment to be hurried past. That is exactly backwards. Christ spoke the pardon first and the cure second, and He said plainly why: the visible healing was given that ye may know the invisible authority. Strip out the forgiveness and the miracle has no point left; it becomes a wonder without a doctrine, a kindness without a Saviour. The health-and-wealth preachers who promise the bed carried away to every believer of sufficient faith have taken the sign and thrown away the thing signified, and they leave their hearers still palsied in the only place that damns.

Recover the order Christ set. Man’s deepest disability is not in his limbs but in his will, which is loosed from God and cannot rise; total depravity means the sinner is not merely weak but bedfast, unable to come unless he is carried. So the friends’ faith is worth marking: they could not cure him, but they could bring him, and Christ honoured the bringing. Intercession is the ministry of the four who tore up the roof. And the word that met the man was sovereign and free — Son, thy sins be forgiven thee — spoken before he asked it, spoken by the One who has power on earth to forgive. When such a word comes, the paralysis of the will breaks, and the man who could not stir rises, takes up his bed, and walks home glorifying God.

Greek & Hebrew Roots

The word is paralysis worn down by English use — the body loosed from the will’s command.

expand to see more

Palsy — a contraction of paralysis, Old French paralisie, Greek paralusis.

The Greek means “a loosing aside” — the limbs unstrung from the will.

The palsied man cannot come; he must be brought (Mar 2:3).

Christ pardoned first and healed second, on purpose (Mar 2:5; Mat 9:6).

The cure was the public receipt of the Son of man’s authority to forgive.

Usage

"Sick of the palsy: the man who cannot rise until Another commands him."

"Son, thy sins be forgiven thee — the pardon came before the bed was ever lifted."

"Christ healed the palsy that men might know He had power on earth to forgive sins."
